question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old right-hand-dominant man with a medical history notable for non-insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic atrial fibrillation on apixaban, stage 2 chronic kidney disease, and remote left hip arthroplasty was transported to the emergency department by county fire EMS after falling approximately 8 feet from an aluminum extension ladder while trimming tree branches in his driveway at 08:10 this morning. A neighbor who heard the crash found him supine on concrete with pruning shears beside him; he was breathing, had a palpable carotid pulse, but his eyes were closed and he produced only low-pitched moans that did not form recognizable words. No seizure-like shaking, tongue biting, or emesis was witnessed and there was no report of headstrike beyond the presumed impact to the occiput when he landed. Paramedics arrived at 08:18, applied a rigid cervical collar, secured him supine to a vacuum mattress with head blocks, placed a 16-gauge IV in the right antecubital fossa but ran only a 10 mL saline lock, and administered no fentanyl, midazolam, ketamine, paralytics, dextrose, naloxone, or vasopressors so that the initial neurologic examination would remain unaltered. A finger-stick glucose was 118 mg/dL, and there was no obvious alcohol odor. During the twelve-minute transport he received 12 L/min oxygen through a non-rebreather mask and remained hemodynamically stable. Upon arrival to our resuscitation bay at 08:34, immediately prior to any hospital therapy, vital signs are blood pressure 146/82 mm Hg obtained in the left brachial artery, heart rate 94 beats per minute in an irregularly irregular rhythm on the monitor, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute with shallow but regular chest rise, oxygen saturation 99 % on the pre-hospital mask, and rectal temperature 36.6 °C. The patient lies motionless on the EMS backboard, work boots still laced, grey sweatshirt damp with morning dew, and a 4-cm linear scalp laceration with scant oozing is noted at the right occipital rim. Initial airway survey shows the mouth partially open with intact dentition, midsize tongue, and dried blood coating the posterior palate; a Yankauer catheter gently suctioning the oropharynx triggers a brisk gag followed by a muffled groan. Throughout quiet observation his eyelids remain firmly shut. When the trauma nurse calls his first and last name at conversational volume there is no change, but after the name is repeated loudly near his right ear both lids part to mid-palpebral distance, revealing pupils 3 mm bilaterally that constrict briskly to direct and consensual light; once questioning ceases, the lids drift closed again. He does not follow commands such as “show two fingers” or “wiggle your toes.” Speech is absent; instead, every 20–30 seconds a deep, throaty moan escapes, devoid of articulation, syllable formation, or recognizable language. Cervical collar remains in place and neck is non-mobile for the exam. Upper extremities lie slack along his torso, but when firm nail-bed pressure is applied to the left index finger both shoulders adduct, elbows sweep rapidly into pronounced flexion, forearms pronate, and wrists flex with fists partially clenched; lower limbs simultaneously extend at the knees with plantar flexion of the ankles. The posture endures two to three seconds beyond cessation of the stimulus before limbs relax back to baseline. A second noxious stimulus—a sternal rub—elicits an identical symmetric response without any purposeful attempt to reach toward or push away the examiner’s hand. Tone between stimuli is otherwise reduced, and no spontaneous movement of the trunk or extremities is observed. Deep tendon reflexes are 3 + at biceps and patellae, 2 + at Achilles; plantar responses are mute. Corneal reflexes are intact, extra-ocular movements appear conjugate when the globes are gently rotated, and a grimace is noted when supra-orbital ridge pressure is applied. Cardiovascular examination reveals an irregularly irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses 2 + with capillary refill <2 seconds. Lungs are clear to auscultation with equal breath sounds and resonant percussion. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender; bowel sounds are present. Pelvis is stable to gentle compression, and rectal tone is preserved. No obvious long-bone deformities are present, though mild ecchymosis is forming over the right olecranon and left lateral thigh. A focused log-roll demonstrates no vertebral step-off or paraspinal hematoma, and posterior chest wall inspection shows scattered superficial abrasions. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes reveals clear lung fields and normal mediastinum; pelvic radiograph is negative for fracture. Point-of-care venous blood gas on the current oxygen flow shows pH 7.36, pCO₂ 41 mm Hg, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Baseline laboratories—including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation profile, serum ethanol level, high-sensitivity troponin, and type & screen—have been drawn but are pending. No analgesics, sedatives, paralytics, hyperosmolar agents, vasopressors, or intravenous fluids have yet been administered in the department, ensuring that the neurologic findings described—eyes that only open after loud verbal stimulus, persistent unintelligible groaning in lieu of speech, and a characteristic bilateral flexor limb reaction to painful stimulation—represent his untreated baseline at presentation. Neurosurgery, trauma surgery, and critical care have been emergently paged; non-contrast head CT, CT angiography of the neck, and whole-spine CT are ordered stat, and serial neurologic checks every fifteen minutes have been instituted while airway equipment is prepared at bedside should his protective reflexes diminish.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye, verbal, and motor responses on the initial unsedated examination.
- Eye opening: opens eyes to a loud voice, not spontaneously → E3.
- Verbal response: moans without recognizable words → V2 (incomprehensible sounds).
- Motor response: pain elicits stereotyped arm adduction, elbow and wrist flexion, and forearm pronation with leg extension. This is abnormal flexion, not withdrawal or localization → M3.
Total = E3 + V2 + M3 = 8.
Final answer: 8
